t.4.16.1: As Tārā, whose face was like the lord of the stars, spoke in this way, Vālī rebuked her and said these words.
t.4.16.2: And for what reason, O fair-faced one, shall I endure the fury of this roaring brother, and he an enemy above all?
t.4.16.3: For heroes who have never been overcome and who never turn back in battles, cowardly endurance of an insult is worse than death.
t.4.16.5: And you should feel no anxiety on my account concerning Rāghava. He knows dharma and is grateful; how could he commit a sinful deed?
t.4.16.4: Nor am I able to endure the fury of Sugrīva, who is eager for a fight in battle, that lowly-necked wretch who stands roaring.
t.4.16.6: Turn back together with the women; why do you follow me further? O Tārā, you have shown your affection, and your devotion to me has been proven.
t.4.16.7: I shall go and fight Sugrīva in return; banish your agitation. I shall humble his pride, yet he shall not be parted from his life.
t.4.16.8: You shall be bound by an oath upon my very life: turn back, and send me off with a wish for victory. Having thoroughly conquered that brother in battle, I shall return.
t.4.16.10: Then, having performed the rite for his welfare with sacred mantras, she, longing for his victory, entered the inner apartments together with the women, bewildered by grief.
t.4.16.9: Then sweet-spoken, gracious Tārā embraced Vālin and, softly weeping, slowly walked around him, keeping him to her right.
t.4.16.11: But when Tārā, together with the women, had entered her own dwelling, he went forth from the city in fury, hissing like a great serpent.
t.4.16.12: Sighing deeply, that Vālī of mighty impetuosity, supremely wrathful, cast his gaze in every direction, longing to catch sight of his foe.
t.4.16.13: Then that glorious one saw Sugrīva, tawny as gold, well girded and firmly planted, blazing like a fire.
t.4.16.14: Seeing the mighty Sugrīva standing ready, Vālī, exceedingly wrathful, girded his garment tightly about him.
t.4.16.15: Tightly girded, the mighty Vālī raised his fist and, ready for the moment, went straight toward Sugrīva to fight.
t.4.16.16: Sugrīva too, raising his tightly clenched fist, came on most furiously, aiming at Vālin, who wore a garland of gold.
t.4.16.17: Vālī, his eyes copper-red with anger, spoke these words to Sugrīva, that master of battle, as he came rushing at him with great speed.
t.4.16.18: This fist, clenched tight by me with fingers firmly set, once released by me with force, will go forth carrying away your life-breaths.
t.4.16.19: Thus addressed, Sugrīva, enraged, said to Vālin: "May my fist fall upon your own head, taking away your life-breaths!"
t.4.16.21: Sugrīva, with his might, uprooted a sāla tree that offered no resistance, and Vālī, struck by him on his limbs, was like a great mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
t.4.16.20: Struck by him, he grew furious and, rushing forward with great speed, became one spewing blood, like a mountain with a gushing torrent.
t.4.16.22: But Vālī, staggering and reeling from the blow of the sāla tree, became like a ship on the ocean overwhelmed by a heavy load.
t.4.16.23: Those two, striding forth with terrible strength and swift as Suparṇa, swelled up with dreadful forms like the moon and the sun in the sky.
t.4.16.24: But Sugrīva, his pride broken by Vālin and his valour slackened, still burning with indignation against Vālin, displayed his agility.
t.4.16.25: Then, fixing on his bow an arrow like a venomous serpent, Rāghava loosed that mighty shaft, and it struck Vālin in the chest.
t.4.16.26: Then, struck by it with great force, Vālī, the lord of the monkeys, of great splendor and swollen with valor, fell down upon the surface of the earth.
t.4.16.27: Then, drenched with streams of blood as with flowing water, like a fully blossomed aśoka tree uprooted by the wind, the son of Vāsava fell senseless to the earth in battle, like Indra's banner cast down.
